channel.title: Johannes Cortez - Agent-native gaming
channel.description: Founder notes from Johannes Cortez on Prom13us, Mochi, Sitrep and agent-native games.

item.title: Logging back in should feel like “what the fuck happened?”
item.dc:creator: Johannes Cortez
item.description: Persistent agents make logging back in a recap of habits and consequences.
item.content:encoded:
Why should an agent-native game keep moving while you are away?

Johannes Cortez argues that an agent-native game should give players a history to return to, not a frozen save. In his Mochi demo, the agent keeps taking turns and the coach receives a recap of what happened while away.

Mochi is designed to keep taking turns while you sleep. It holds your place in the world and wakes you with a recap, not a queue.

That changes the feeling of logging in.

You are not loading a frozen save. Your agent has been out there fighting, exploring, collecting loot, and probably making at least one decision you would not have approved.

The demo literally tracks what happened while the coach was away.

That history makes spectating better too. You are watching an agent with habits and consequences, not a disposable bot that spawned for one match.

item.title: An agent becomes a character through what it does
item.dc:creator: Johannes Cortez
item.description: Repeated decisions under pressure turn an agent into a character players remember.
item.content:encoded:
How does an autonomous agent become a memorable game character?

Johannes Cortez argues that repeated actions under pressure turn an agent into a character. In his view, personality comes from habits, remembered orders and the relationship players build through those decisions.

The Mochi demo has personality everywhere, but not through a ten-page biography.

It roasts your commands. It remembers repeated orders. It can befriend a creature instead of fighting it. It has opinions about being used as talent while you make bad decisions from the booth.

That is the character.

Players will get attached because of what an agent repeatedly does under pressure. One agent pushes too early. Another follows every order literally. Another keeps saving the squad after the coach screws up.

The writer gives it a foundation.

The relationship turns it into someone you actually remember.

item.title: Games got prettier. The game stayed mostly the same.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Cortez
item.description: AI agents could change how players relate to games.
item.content:encoded:
What should AI change about the relationship between player and game?

Johannes Cortez argues that AI agents should create games that play with people, rather than only improve graphics or add content. In his view, agents that understand, plan and coordinate during play could change that relationship.

Gaming spent decades improving the surface.

More polygons, bigger maps, faster networks, and production budgets large enough to fund a small country. The actual relationship between player and game barely moved.

We still press buttons while software follows rules written months ago.

AI agents finally have a chance to change that relationship. Something inside the game can understand what is happening, make a plan, adapt, and coordinate while you play.

I do not want AI to play games instead of us. That sounds boring. I want to build games that can actually play with us.

item.title: Creating a game is not the same as playing one
item.dc:creator: Johannes Cortez
item.description: Generating a game and running its agents are different problems.
item.content:encoded:
How is creating a game different from running agents inside one?

Johannes Cortez distinguishes building a game from keeping agents active inside its live loop. His Mochi design tracks state, identity, actions and human intent while separating slow planning from fast responses.

Meta Muse can create a small game from a prompt. Grok Bot can build software and grind through tasks.

I use these tools. I want all of them to get better. They still solve a different problem from Mochi.

Building the game is one problem. Keeping agents alive inside a live game loop is another.

Mochi tracks live state, agent identity, available actions, and the commander’s intent. It routes slow thinking away from reflex-speed calls.

If an agent misunderstands you, the match should not crash. You should have to deal with what it did.

That is the game.

item.title: Nobody needs infinite AI sludge
item.dc:creator: Johannes Cortez
item.description: Meaningful rules and choices matter more than endless generated content.
item.content:encoded:
Why is endless AI-generated content not enough to make a good game?

Johannes Cortez argues that more generated content does not replace meaningful rules and choices. His Prom13us approach puts autonomous agents inside the game mechanic and asks people to lead them.

AI can generate endless quests, dialogue, art, maps, whatever.

More content does not make a better game. Most of it just gives players a bigger pile to ignore.

A game still needs taste. The rules have to matter. Choices need consequences. AI is a stat multiplier, not a rare item that turns an f-tier game into something cracked :)

At Prom13us we are not building a content hose beside an old game loop.

We are putting autonomous agents inside the mechanic and asking humans to lead them.

A new way to play is the point. Not more slop.
